  The Reject Inference (RI) problem asks how to (partially) correct the acceptance
  decision induced bias in classification problems, by leveraging information
  of rejected applicants, even though their outcome is unknown. This thesis introduces
  a dynamic perspective on RI by arguing that discrepancies between the expected
  performance of a classifier (e.g., estimated through cross-validation) and its
  realized performance over future acceptance rounds constitute a signal, which I term
  *surprise*, that allows to evidence the acceptance bias. First, the RI problem is
  formulated within a measure-theoretic framework to make every underlying assumption
  explicit. Second, the central hypothesis of surprise as a signal to observe the bias is formulated.
  Third a careful simulation study evidencing the viability is presented. Finally,
  an outlook on possible applications is proposed to exploit the signal.
